payload.title: Write-Ahead Logging
payload.author: SQLite
payload.note: Explain the core mechanism, the concurrency benefit, and the checkpoint tradeoff.
payload.extracted_text: SQLite's default rollback journal writes original pages to a journal before changing the database. Write-ahead logging reverses that sequence: changes are appended to a separate WAL file while the original database remains unchanged. A transaction commits when its commit record is appended to the WAL. Readers remember an end mark and reconstruct a consistent view using pages from the WAL up to that mark, falling back to the database file for pages not present there. This allows readers and a writer to operate at the same time, though there can still be only one writer. A checkpoint later transfers WAL content back into the database file. Checkpointing can pause when it reaches WAL content newer than an active reader's end mark, and long-running readers can prevent a checkpoint from completing. By default SQLite automatically checkpoints around 1000 pages. WAL normally needs all processes to share memory on the same host and is not intended for a network filesystem. Source captured from SQLite's official WAL documentation on 2026-09-21.
